question: Why is reusing disposable syringes dangerous in the clinic?
explanation: Reusing syringes transfers residual blood and infectious agents directly from one patient to another. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h1)

question: Which of these is an unsafe injection practice?

options.A: Administering medication with a newly opened sterile syringe
options.B: Using a single multidose vial for multiple patients without a sterile barrier
options.C: Recapping needles using a single-handed scoop method
options.D: Disposing of sharp containers when they reach the three-quarters full mark

explanation: Multidose vials can become contaminated and spread infections if proper sterile techniques are ignored between patients. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h1)

question: Which action causes the most accidental needle-stick injuries for nurses?
explanation: Attempting to replace the cap on a used needle frequently results in missed caps and finger punctures. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h2)

question: Why are student nurses often more vulnerable to sharp injuries during clinical postings?

options.A: Hospital management provides them with inferior protective equipment
options.B: Standard safety guidelines do not apply to learners
options.C: They possess less familiarity with safe handling habits under pressure
options.D: They handle a higher volume of patients than senior staff

explanation: Inexperience combined with anxiety during busy shifts leads to hurried and unsafe sharp handling. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h2)

question: A patient in a poorly resourced clinic is most at risk for which hazard?

options.A: Chronic respiratory failure from oral tablets
options.B: Severe allergic reactions to sterile water
options.D: Nosocomial transmission via reused injection devices

explanation: Supply shortages sometimes tempt settings to reuse single-use items, which spreads blood infections. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h3)

question: Using one multidose medication vial for multiple patients is risky because of...

options.A: Rapid chemical breakdown of the drug in tropical climates
options.B: Excessive financial cost to the hospital pharmacy
options.C: Unpredictable absorption rates in elderly patients
options.D: Potential backflow of blood or contaminants into the shared vial

explanation: Microorganisms from one patient can enter the shared vial via contaminated needles and infect subsequent recipients. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h3)

question: Who is at the highest risk for needle-stick injuries outside the hospital setting?

options.A: Local food vendors operating near markets
options.B: Primary school teachers in rural communities
options.C: Informal waste pickers and municipal refuse collectors
options.D: Agricultural workers tending to crop fields

explanation: Waste handlers frequently encounter loose sharps that were improperly mixed with household garbage. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h4)

question: How do improperly disposed medical sharps end up in community waste?

options.A: Returning expired medications to the hospital pharmacy
options.B: Transporting sealed sharp containers to central landfills
options.C: Placing used syringes into normal household trash bags
options.D: Burning safety boxes in high-temperature incinerators

explanation: Throwing sharps into regular bins bypasses specialized medical waste pathways, endangering sanitation workers. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h4)

question: What is the correct action immediately after giving an injection?

options.A: Leave the syringe on the bedside tray for later collection
options.B: Break the needle off the barrel by hand to save space
options.C: Place the plastic cap back on the needle using both hands
options.D: Drop the used syringe directly into a rigid safety box

explanation: Immediate disposal into a puncture-resistant container prevents accidental injury to staff and patients. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h5)

question: Why are auto-disable syringes effective in preventing bloodborne infections?

options.A: They neutralize viruses instantly upon contact with medication
options.B: They eliminate the need for any sharps disposal containers
options.C: They automatically lock or break after a single use, stopping reuse
options.D: They dissolve completely in water within several minutes

explanation: Auto-disable mechanisms make it mechanically impossible to draw up medication a second time with the same syringe. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h5)

question: What is the first step a nurse should take after a needle-stick injury?

options.A: Apply a concentrated bleach solution to the puncture wound
options.B: Report immediately to the hospital medical director
options.C: Squeeze the wound forcefully to force out contaminated blood
options.D: Wash the affected area thoroughly with soap and water

explanation: Washing with soap and water removes surface contaminants without causing further local tissue trauma. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h6)

question: Why is squeezing a needle-stick wound discouraged during first aid?

options.A: It causes permanent nerve paralysis in the affected digit
options.B: It neutralizes the effectiveness of subsequent antiseptic washes
options.C: It damages delicate local capillaries and increases pathogen absorption
options.D: It delays the administration of oral antibiotic therapy

explanation: Aggressive squeezing traumatizes tissue and can force infectious fluids deeper into the vascular bed. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h6)
